\chapter{Es- --- the Vowel Spanish Put in Front}
\label{ch:es-inicial}
\hlchaptermodality{30}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can strip the e- from a Spanish word beginning es- plus a consonant and recognise the English word underneath.}

Decode estacion, estudiante and espacio by taking the e- off the front.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[es- + consonant]{es- + consonant}

\label{lesson:ES-C57-es-inicial}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} — the one about how and where. (\emph{Estar}.) Now say \textquotedblleft{}to study.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Estudiar}.)

You have known both since your first chapters. Today they explain each other.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a word cannot start like that}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Latin words beginning \emph{s} + a consonant grew an \emph{e-} in front.}
\end{quote}

Latin was happy to start a word with \emph{st-}, \emph{sp-} or \emph{sc-}. Spanish was not — the mouth wants a vowel there — so it put one in.

\begin{quote}
\emph{stāre} $\to$ \textbf{es}tar  ·  \emph{studēre} $\to$ \textbf{es}tudiar
\end{quote}

Nothing was added to the meaning. A vowel was added to the \emph{front}, because the alternative was a beginning Spanish could not say.

English borrowed the very same Latin words and never needed the vowel:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{from} & \textbf{English kept it bare} \\
\midrule
\emph{estar} & \emph{stāre} & \textbf{state}, \textbf{stay}, \textbf{status} \\
\emph{estudiar} & \emph{studēre} & \textbf{study}, \textbf{student}, \textbf{studio} \\
\emph{escuela} & \emph{schola} & \textbf{school}, \textbf{scholar} \\
\emph{especial} & \emph{speciālis} & \textbf{special}, \textbf{species} \\
\emph{espíritu} & \emph{spīritus} & \textbf{spirit} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the rule runs in both directions, and the backwards one is the useful one: \textbf{take the \emph{e-} off the front, and an English word is often standing there.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Take the \emph{e-} off and say what you see.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{estación} $\to$ \textbf{st}ación $\to$ \textbf{station}
  \item \emph{estudiante} $\to$ \textbf{st}udiante $\to$ \textbf{student}
  \item \emph{espacio} $\to$ \textbf{sp}acio $\to$ \textbf{space}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Estación} took two rules at once: the \emph{e-} came off the front, and the \emph{-ción} you learned seven chapters ago became \emph{-tion} at the back. That is what these rules are for — they stack.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{A word you would expect to fit, and it does not.}

\emph{Español} looks like a perfect example. It is not. Its \emph{Es-} is not an added vowel — it is what is left of Latin \emph{\textbf{Hispānia}}, whose \emph{H} was already silent. \emph{España} is \emph{Hispania} with the \emph{h} gone, not \emph{spaña} with an \emph{e} glued on.

So check before you claim one. The rule is about words that \emph{began} with two consonants in Latin. When the \emph{e} was there all along, there is nothing to take off.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the rule in your own words.

Then take the \emph{e-} off \emph{estilo} and say the English word you find. (\emph{Style}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
